title: Your Nitnem now
hookLine: write down what your daily prayer is now, however small

lines: WHAT DO YOU ACTUALLY DO, MOST DAYS?
cards: An honest question, the kind a friend asks on a long walk: what do you actually do, most days? Not what you planned in January. What really happens on an ordinary Wednesday, between waking and sleep?
Maybe one breath before you reach for your phone. Maybe a shabad on the drive to work. Maybe nothing yet.
Every one of those is a real answer. Today, a word Sikhs use for that question, and a pen. Nitnem.

teach.h: NIT AND NEM: DAILY, AND A RULE.
teach.b: Nitnem means the daily rule. In Punjabi, nit is daily, and nem is a rule or a vow.

teach.h: THE REHAT'S NITNEM: MORNING, DUSK, NIGHT.
teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada published by the SGPC, sets out a Nitnem: the Japji, the Jaap and the ten Savaiye in the morning, Rehras at dusk, Kirtan Sohila at night.
Some Sikhs also say Chaupai and Anand in the morning. That's the full shape, the banis from two days ago. Initiated Sikhs take it on as part of their rehat.
Others grow into it slowly: a grandmother who says all of it before dawn, a student who listens to the Japji on the bus, a father who says Sohila beside a child's bed.

Sikh teaching gives a reason the rule matters, and it isn't keeping score. In the Japji, Guru Nanak names the amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, as the time to dwell on the true Name and the greatness of God.
A rule is a way of keeping that appointment on mornings when the feeling isn't there.
And Sikhs say just as plainly that recitation without attention is hollow; the Savaiye you learned this year make that point about ritual without love.

teach.h: THE RULE AND THE HEART, TOGETHER.
teach.b: The rule and the heart are meant to travel together. For someone learning about this path, or walking beside a Sikh partner or parent, a daily practice might start very small: a line, a minute, a shabad.

Sikhs who keep the full Nitnem would add that the full one is the rehat for the initiated, and a small start is a start, not the whole. The app isn't setting a rule today. It's asking what yours is, right now, honestly.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada sets a daily Nitnem of morning banis, Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila at night; initiated Sikhs keep it as part of their discipline, and many others build toward it at their own pace.

games.q: it's a heavy week, and the morning prayers feel empty. what does Sikh teaching hold together here?
o: stop until the feeling comes back.
keep the appointment, and bring what attention you can.
say the words faster to get through them.
games.why: the Japji names the amritvela as a daily appointment, and the Savaiye warn that ritual without love is empty: Sikhs keep both the rule and the heart.

practice: On paper or in your notes app, write two words at the top, my nitnem, and underneath, what you actually do now, however small: one breath and Waheguru, the Japji on Sundays, Rehras playing while you cook, or nothing yet, but I'd like one line in the morning.
Keep it true, not impressive. Then read it once and sit with it, without grading it.

wordCard.voice: Nitnem, the daily rule: for Sikhs, the set banis of morning, dusk and night; and today, the honest shape of what you do each day.

orig.note: Punjabi: the daily rule, the banis a Sikh says each day.
